details:
**Mont Blanc**
The highest mountain in the Alps and in Western Europe, at about 15,775 feet (4,808 m), on the border of France and Italy. Its name means "White Mountain," after its permanent ice dome. Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard first climbed it in 1786. France and Italy still dispute exactly where the border runs near the summit, and two Air India planes crashed on the mountain, in 1950 and 1966.

**Matterhorn**
The famous pyramid-shaped peak with steep faces on the Swiss–Italian border above Zermatt. It is one of the most frequent giveaways for the range.

**Chamonix and the first Winter Olympics**
Chamonix is a French resort town at the foot of Mont Blanc. It hosted the first Winter Olympic Games in 1924. Other Alpine ski resorts include Courmayeur (Italy), and Kitzbühel, St. Anton, and Innsbruck (Austria).

**Ötzi the Iceman**
A natural mummy of a man from the Copper Age, about 5,300 years old. Hikers found him in 1991 in a glacier in the Ötztal Alps on the Austria–Italy border. He is now displayed in Bolzano, Italy.

**Great St. Bernard Pass**
An ancient pass between Switzerland's Valais and Italy's Aosta Valley, on the ridge between Mont Blanc and Monte Rosa. Napoleon led his army over it in 1800, an event Jacques-Louis David painted in Napoleon Crossing the Alps. The hospice there gave its name to the St. Bernard dog.

**Brenner Pass**
One of the lowest and busiest passes through the Alps. It links Innsbruck in Austria with Bolzano in Italy's South Tyrol.

**Crossing of the Alps by Hannibal**
In 218 BC, during the Second Punic War, the Carthaginian general Hannibal led his army, including war elephants, across the Alps into the Po Valley to invade Italy. His brother Hasdrubal later made his own crossing. Other famous crossings include Napoleon's, Theodoric the Great's invasion of Italy, and Russian general Alexander Suvorov's 1799 campaign through Switzerland over passes such as the Panix.

**Gotthard Base Tunnel**
A railway tunnel about 57 km (35 miles) long under the Swiss Alps, opened in 2016. It is the longest and deepest railway tunnel in the world. The Lötschberg Base Tunnel under the Bernese Alps is another long Swiss base tunnel.

**Sources of the Rhine and the Rhône**
Both rivers begin in the Swiss Alps. The Rhône starts at the Rhône Glacier and flows through Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean. The Rhine flows north to the North Sea. The Aletsch Glacier, the largest in the Alps, drains into the Rhône.

**Dolomites**
A range of pale, jagged limestone (dolomite) peaks in northeastern Italy, part of the Southern Alps and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**Julian Alps and Triglav**
The southeastern subrange of the Alps, reaching into Slovenia and named after Julius Caesar. Its highest peak, Triglav, is the center of Triglav National Park, where the Soča River begins.

**Four-thousanders, Monte Rosa, and Piz Bernina**
The Alps contain all of Western Europe's peaks over 4,000 meters, including Monte Rosa (the second-highest), the Weisshorn, and Piz Bernina (the highest in the Eastern Alps). Karl Blodig was the first person to climb all of the major Alpine four-thousanders.

**Grossglockner and the Hohe Tauern**
The Grossglockner is the highest mountain in Austria. It is in the Hohe Tauern range of the Central Eastern Alps, south of the Salzach River valley.

**Eiger**
A peak in the Bernese Alps of Switzerland, famous for its huge and deadly north face (the Nordwand), the largest north face in the Alps.

**Alpine orogeny**
The mountain-building event in which the African plate collided with the Eurasian plate and formed the Alps. The same orogeny folded other structures in Europe, such as the Weald–Artois Anticline in England and France.
